title: How to Build a Solid Pool Bridge and Stance (Beginner Guide)
description: Learn how to set your stance, make open and closed bridges, and use three quick drills to shoot straighter and steadier at pool.
body:
Want to know the quickest way to make a pool player better? It is not a fancy cue or a secret stroke. It is a boring-sounding thing most beginners skip: a steady stance and a solid bridge. Get those two right and everything else gets easier, from straight pots to controlling the cue ball. With the Mosconi Cup heading to Orlando on November 27-30, it is a great moment to watch how the pros stay rock-still on every shot and copy the basics.

What is the bridge, and why does it matter?

The bridge is the hand you rest on the table to guide the front of your cue. Think of it as a tiny track for the stick. If the track wobbles, the cue wobbles, and the cue ball goes where you did not plan. A good bridge keeps the cue level, lined up and gliding forward on the same path every time.

Your stance is the base that holds it all together. A stable base means your body stays quiet while only your arm swings the cue.

Step 1: Build your stance

Start by standing behind the shot, looking along the line from the cue ball to your target. Then step into it the same way each time.

  • Feet: Place your back foot roughly in line with the shot, with your front foot a comfortable step ahead and angled slightly out. Many players use about shoulder width, then adjust to feel balanced.
  • Knees: Keep your back leg fairly straight and bend the front knee a little. This is what lets you lower your body without wobbling.
  • Chin: Lower your head so your chin is close to the cue. Your dominant eye should sit right above or near the stick.
  • Cue arm: Let your forearm hang down so the cue is held at about a right angle to it when you hit the ball.

Comfort is the test. If you feel like you are about to tip over, widen your feet or lower your hips a bit.

Step 2: Make an open bridge

The open bridge is the easiest place to start, and plenty of strong players use it for everyday shots.

  1. Place your hand flat on the table, a few inches behind the cue ball.
  2. Spread your fingers a little so your hand feels like a small tripod.
  3. Raise your thumb and tuck it against the side of your first finger to create a V-shaped groove.
  4. Rest the cue in that groove and slide it back and forth a few times to check it moves smoothly.

A bridge that is too tight grips the cue and makes the stroke jerky. Too loose and the stick wanders. Aim for firm but relaxed.

Step 3: Try a closed bridge

A closed bridge wraps your first finger around the cue to form a loop. Many players like it for extra control on power shots or when they want the cue to stay locked in line. To try it, make the open bridge, then curl your index finger over the top of the cue and bring it toward your thumb. Do not squeeze. The loop is a guide, not a clamp.

Neither bridge is better for everyone. Try both and use the one that feels more consistent.

Bridge distance: how far from the cue ball?

A common starting point is about six to eight inches between your bridge hand and the cue ball. Shorter bridges can feel steadier on soft shots and delicate position play. Longer bridges give you a smoother swing on power shots. Experiment and notice what keeps your cue most level.

Three quick drills to lock it in

  • The freeze drill: Take your stance and bridge, then hold perfectly still for three seconds before shooting. If you wobble, reset.
  • The follow-through hold: After each shot, keep your cue pointed down the line and freeze until the object ball stops. It trains a quiet body.
  • The rail slide: Practice sliding the cue through your bridge along a line on the table without a ball, 20 smooth strokes in a row.

Doing even ten minutes of these before you play can make a surprising difference within a week.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Standing too upright: You see less of the line and lose stability.
  • Moving your head during the stroke: Stay down until the shot is finished.
  • Gripping too hard: A tight back hand ruins smoothness. Hold the cue like you are holding a small bird.
  • Changing your bridge every shot: Pick a routine and repeat it.

Watch the pros and borrow the routine

Next time you watch a top-level match, ignore the ball for a moment and watch the player's body. Notice how little moves besides the cue arm. The Mosconi Cup is a fun showcase for that kind of calm under pressure. Check the Mosconi Cup 2026 page for dates and schedule details, browse upcoming events on the tournaments page, see the big tournaments list, and keep the calendar handy so you never miss a match worth studying.

Final thoughts

A solid stance and bridge will not make you a champion overnight, but it is the foundation every champion shares. Spend a few sessions making it automatic and your potting, cue ball control and confidence will all move up a level. Which do you prefer, open bridge or closed bridge?
